items.q: What does a dose-response curve show?
options: The percent of a test population that responds at each dose
How long a substance stays in the body after one dose
The concentration of a substance at each level of a food chain
The number of test animals used at each dose

why.correct: A dose-response curve plots dose (often mg/kg) against the percent of a test group showing a response, such as death or illness.
options: Right: dose goes on the horizontal axis and the percent responding on the vertical axis.
Time in the body is not on a dose-response curve; dose and response are.
That describes biomagnification, not a dose-response curve.
Group size is part of the design; the curve shows the percent that respond.

items.q: On a dose-response curve, what is the threshold dose?
options: The dose at which half of the test animals die
The highest dose at which no response is seen
The largest dose that was tested in the study
The dose at which about 99% of test animals die

why.correct: The threshold dose is where the curve leaves zero: below it, no effect is observed in the test group.
options: That is the LD50, read at 50% on the response axis.
Right: below the threshold, the test group shows no measurable effect.
The largest dose tested is the end of the curve, not its threshold.
At the top of the curve nearly all animals respond; the threshold is at the bottom.

items.q: What is the difference between an ED50 and an LD50?
options: ED50 is measured in mg and LD50 in mg/kg of body mass
ED50 is the dose that kills 50 animals, and LD50 kills 50%
ED50 is for a nonlethal effect in half the group; LD50 is for death
ED50 is read from the top of a curve, and LD50 from the bottom

why.correct: ED50 is the dose that produces a set, nonlethal effect (sleep, rash, lower growth) in half of a test group; LD50 is the dose that kills half.
options: Both are usually given in mg per kg of body mass.
Both refer to 50% of a test group, not to a count of 50 animals.
Right: ED50 is the effective dose 50%, for an effect such as illness; LD50 is the lethal dose 50%.
Both are read where the curve crosses 50% on the response axis.

items.q: Some substances, including many that cause cancer, are treated as having no threshold dose. What does this mean for the shape of their dose-response curve?
options: The curve stays flat at zero until the dose reaches the LD50
The curve has no 50% point, so no LD50 can be measured
The curve falls as the dose rises, so larger doses do less harm
Risk rises from zero with any dose, so no dose is assumed safe

why.correct: A threshold is a flat stretch at zero response. Without one, regulators assume the risk grows from zero with any exposure.
options: A flat stretch at zero is a threshold, the opposite of no threshold.
A no-threshold curve can still cross 50%; the term is about the low end.
Responses rise with dose on these curves; the issue is where the rise begins.
Right: with no threshold, even a small dose is assumed to carry some risk.

items.q: What is the LD50 of pesticide Y in the fish?

why.correct: Pesticide Y kills 50% of the fish at 40 mg/kg, so its LD50 is 40 mg/kg.

mistakes.why: That is the LD50 of pesticide X. Use the column for pesticide Y: it reaches 50% killed at 40 mg/kg.
50 is the percent killed, not the dose. Find the row where 50% of the fish die and read its dose.

items.q: From the table, what is the threshold dose for pesticide X: the highest dose tested that killed no fish?

why.correct: Pesticide X kills 0% at 0, 10 and 20 mg/kg and 2% at 30 mg/kg, so its threshold lies at 20 mg/kg (between 20 and 30).

mistakes.why: At 30 mg/kg, 2% of the fish died, so that dose is above the threshold. The last dose with 0% killed is 20 mg/kg.
10 mg/kg is the threshold for pesticide Y. For X, no fish die at 20 mg/kg either.

items.q: Which statement compares the two pesticides correctly?
options: X is twice as toxic as Y, since its LD50 is twice as large
They are equally toxic, since both kill about 98% or more of the fish at 160 mg/kg
Y is twice as toxic as X: its LD50 is half of X’s
X is more toxic, since its curve keeps rising to a higher dose

why.correct: Compare LD50s by division: $\frac{80\,\text{mg/kg}}{40\,\text{mg/kg}} = 2$, so Y is twice as toxic.
options: A larger LD50 means more pesticide is needed to kill, so X is less toxic.
Toxicity is compared at the 50% point, where Y needs half the dose X does.
Right: the LD50 of Y is 40 mg/kg and of X is 80 mg/kg, and $\frac{80}{40} = 2$.
X rises later because it is less toxic; more of it is needed for the same effect.

items.q: A farmer worries about runoff of pesticide X into a pond. Using the LD50 from the table, write the setup for the dose of X, in milligrams, expected to kill half of a group of 0.60 kg fish. Then give the answer.

mistakes.why: 40 mg/kg is the LD50 of pesticide Y. The question is about X, whose LD50 is 80 mg/kg.
Dividing by body mass leaves mg/kg². Multiply the LD50 by the mass so kilograms cancel.
That uses the LD50 of Y (40 mg/kg). Pesticide X has an LD50 of 80 mg/kg: 80 mg/kg × 0.60 kg = 48 mg.

items.q: A town must choose one of the two pesticides for fields that drain into a fish pond. Based only on these data, which choice is better for the fish, and why?
options: X, because a larger dose of it is needed before fish start to die
Y, because its curve reaches 100% faster, so it breaks down sooner
Y, because it kills fish at lower doses, so less of it reaches the pond
Either one, because both kill about 98% or more of the fish at high doses

why.correct: At every dose from 20 to 80 mg/kg, Y kills a larger percent of fish than X, and its threshold and LD50 are both lower.
options: Right: X has the higher threshold (about 20 mg/kg) and the higher LD50 (80 mg/kg).
How fast a curve rises with dose says nothing about how fast the pesticide breaks down.
Killing fish at lower doses makes Y more dangerous to them, not less.
At the doses most likely in runoff, the low end of the curves, Y kills far more fish.

items.q: Read the graph. What is the ED50 of the sedative for putting mice to sleep?

why.correct: The sleep curve crosses 50% at 10 mg/kg, so the ED50 is 10 mg/kg.

mistakes.why: 60 mg/kg is where half the mice die, the LD50. The ED50 is on the sleep curve, at 50% of mice asleep.
At 5 mg/kg only 10% of the mice sleep. Go up to 50% on the sleep curve and read the dose.

items.q: What is the LD50 of the sedative in mice?

why.correct: The death curve crosses 50% at 60 mg/kg, so the LD50 is 60 mg/kg.

mistakes.why: 10 mg/kg is the ED50, where half the mice sleep. The LD50 is on the death curve.
50 is the percent on the vertical axis. Read the dose where the death curve crosses 50%.

items.q: How many times larger is the LD50 than the ED50 for this sedative?

why.correct: $\frac{60\,\text{mg/kg}}{10\,\text{mg/kg}} = 6$: the lethal dose for half the mice is six times the dose that puts half to sleep.

mistakes.why: A difference (50 mg/kg) does not say how many times larger. Divide: 60 mg/kg ÷ 10 mg/kg = 6.
You divided the ED50 by the LD50. Put the larger dose on top: 60 ÷ 10 = 6.

items.q: Up to what dose do the data show no deaths, even though many mice are asleep?
options: 20 mg/kg, the threshold dose for death
10 mg/kg, where half the mice fall asleep
60 mg/kg, where half the mice die
5 mg/kg, the smallest dose given

why.correct: The threshold for death is where the death curve leaves zero: 20 mg/kg. The gap between the two curves is why the drug can be used.
options: Right: the death curve stays at 0% up to 20 mg/kg, while 95% of mice sleep at that dose.
At 10 mg/kg no mice die, but the death curve stays at zero beyond that too.
At 60 mg/kg half the mice die; deaths start above 20 mg/kg.
Deaths stay at zero well past 5 mg/kg, up to 20 mg/kg.

items.q: A typical dose-response curve for deaths is S-shaped. What happens near the top of the curve?
options: It drops back toward zero as animals build up tolerance
It levels off near 100% as nearly all animals respond
It rises fastest, since large doses act most quickly
It crosses 50%, which marks the threshold dose

why.correct: An S-shaped curve is flat at the bottom (below the threshold), steep in the middle (around 50%) and flat at the top (nearly all respond).
options: The percent responding does not fall as the dose rises on these curves.
Right: once almost all animals respond, larger doses add little.
The steepest part is in the middle, around 50%; the top flattens out.
The 50% point marks the LD50 and is in the middle; the threshold is at the bottom.

items.q: Put the steps for reading an LD50 off a dose-response curve in order.
options: Find 50% on the vertical (response) axis
Go straight across to the curve
Go straight down from that point to the dose axis
Read the dose and write it with its unit, mg/kg

why.correct: Across from 50%, down to the dose axis, then read the value with its unit.

items.q: A new herbicide has an LD50 of 2,400 mg/kg in rats, which seems low in toxicity. Which further information would help judge whether it is safe to spray near homes? Select all that apply.
options: Its threshold dose for effects other than death, such as harm to the liver
Whether it causes cancer or birth defects after years of small doses
The color of the spray when it is mixed with water
How many rats were used in the LD50 test

why.correct: LD50 counts only deaths from one dose. Thresholds for other effects and long-term effects show harm that happens below the LD50.
options: Right: harm can start at doses far below the dose that kills.
Right: harm from years of small doses does not show up in a one-time LD50 test.
Color does not tell you anything about how toxic the herbicide is.
Group size affects how reliable the LD50 is, but it does not add a new kind of harm.

items.q: Explain, using the two-pesticide data, why pesticide Y is a bigger threat to the fish in a pond that gets small amounts of runoff.

why.correct: The lower end of the curves decides what small doses do: Y starts killing fish below 20 mg/kg, X above 20 mg/kg.

specific.frame: Because ___, a small dose of runoff ___, so ___.

cause.label: Cause
options: pesticide Y has a lower threshold and a lower LD50 than X
pesticide Y has a higher LD50 than X
pesticide Y is sprayed on more fields

why.1: Y’s LD50 is 40 mg/kg and X’s is 80 mg/kg, so Y’s is lower, not higher.
why.2: The data compare doses and deaths, not how much is sprayed.

effect.label: Effect
options: kills some fish with Y but none with X
kills the same share of fish with either pesticide
kills fewer fish with Y than with X

why.1: At 20 mg/kg, Y kills 8% of fish and X kills none.
why.2: At low doses Y kills more fish, not fewer.

specific.model: Because pesticide Y has a lower threshold and a lower LD50 than X, a small dose of runoff such as 20 mg/kg kills 8% of the fish with Y but none with X, so Y increases fish deaths at doses where X does no harm.
